author: Reuters
description:
German company faced 65,000 claims from people who said they developed cancer after using weedkiller

A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade.

Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.

Continue reading...
title: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer

author: Agence France-Presse
description:
• Bowler throws support behind Australia’s embattled Test captain

  • Cricket Australia expected to reinforce support of Cummins

Josh Hazlewood has thrown his full support behind Pat Cummins, denying they knew anything about “sandpapergate” while suggesting he could quit if any action was taken against the embattled Australian Test captain.

Cummins has been under huge pressure since Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town in 2018.

Continue reading...
title: Josh Hazlewood suggests he could quit if any action taken against Pat Cummins over ‘sandpapergate’

author: PA, AFP and Guardian sport
description:
• England forward limped off early in 1-1 draw with Cologne

  • Club statement confirms ‘tear of ligament in left ankle’

Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted with the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, saying afterwards that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

More details to follow

Continue reading...
title: Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ after ankle ligament injury in Bayern Munich draw

author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
description:
Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.

Continue reading...
title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer

author: Ben Doherty in New York
description:
Costa Rican diplomat remains frontrunner but needs to win over two more permanent members of security council

The UK and France are believed to have effectively vetoed a controversial United Arab Emirates diplomat in a vote for the next UN secretary general, ostensibly over the UAE’s alleged links to atrocities in Sudan.

The search for a new chief diplomat for the world remained deadlocked on Friday after the UN security council’s ninth straw poll once again did not settle on a candidate.

Continue reading...
title: UK and France believed to have vetoed UAE choice for UN secretary general

author: Sarah Dempster
description:
The comic is sublime as a middle-aged landlord attempting to befriend student tenants. It’s very sweet – but the storylines and supporting characters are flimsy to say the least

Bill Beam (Rob Brydon) is a chump, a sap, a bejumpered limpet clinging to the peripheries of his own existence. “I’m being left behind,” he tells best friend Drew (Kevin Eldon) who, having heard this – and that, and the other – a thousand times before, stifles a well-earned yawn. Bill’s wife has left him for the gardener (“No hard feelings!”) and lo, this ever-dimming bulb of cable-knit neediness must find a solution to both his newfound “cashflow crisis” and deepening existential haplessness. What to do?

Enter, stage left, a fire at the local student halls and, with it, an answer to the plonker’s prayers: Bill will rent out his spare bedrooms to four undergraduates. Yes! This will provide him with the requisite dosh, a much-needed sense of purpose and a fresh audience for his piping-hot takes o
title: Bill’s Included review – Rob Brydon’s new character is as glorious as Gavin & Stacey’s Uncle Bryn

author: Greg Whitmore
description:
Photographer who captured the humanity of subjects including Queen Elizabeth II, Dirk Bogarde, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Tom Stoppard

In 1963, the photographer Dmitri Kasterine heard that Stanley Kubrick was in London filming Dr Strangelove. Kasterine was a fan, so he approached the editor of Queen magazine and successfully pitched a feature on the director at work. Kubrick noticed him on set and said: “Would you like to come and work for me? You stand in the right place.”

Kasterine worked for Kubrick from 1963 to 1971, taking the stills on Dr Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey and A Clockwork Orange. Kubrick taught the photographer the importance of courage, patience and perseverance.

Continue rea
title: Dmitri Kasterine obituary

author: Robert Kitson
description:
Discipline, bench impact and the breakdown will be pivotal in what home captain Maro Itoje says is a ‘massive game’

In the brave new world of the Nations Championship things are not as black and white as they used to be. Of course, England against New Zealand still has its own unique rattle and hum but the context is now slightly different. The winners of the Hillary Shield will have to wait a few hours until Ireland have faced South Africa and France have played Argentina to find out precisely where they stand.

Should the All Blacks triumph with a try bonus point they will be into next Sunday’s grand final regardless of how South Africa fare in Dublin. An England victory, on the other hand, would boost the Springboks and potentially set up a second successive showdown with New Zealand within eight days.

Continue reading...
title: England and New Zealand collide with final spots and reputations on the line

author: Alex Daniel
description:
Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6%

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.

Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

Continue reading...
title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks

author: Jim Powell
description:
Trump in China, blackouts in Kyiv, Israeli strikes in Gaza and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI – the past seven days as captured by the world’s leading photojournalists

Warning: this gallery contains images some readers may find distressing

Continue reading...
title: The week around the world in 20 pictures

author: Benjamin Lee
description:
Christmas comedy hit is set for a follow-up from the point of view of the father with Seth Rogen as writer and producer

A Home Alone sequel is reportedly in development with original star Macaulay Culkin set to return.

According to Puck’s Matthew Belloni, Culkin met with Disney executives earlier this year with a pitch for a follow-up and now the project has been met with a green light. The new Home Alone film will bring the 46-year-old back to the franchise as Kevin McCallister for a comedy that, according to Deadline, will be from the father’s point of view.

Continue reading...
title: Home Alone sequel reportedly in development with Macaulay Culkin returning

author: John Crace
description:
The passionate PM was unafraid to rush in. This could be the start of something lasting … if people could conquer their trust issues

Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire.

But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. A far cry from th
title: Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful EU throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart | John Crace

author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
description:
PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope

Several sentences in to a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Continue reading...
title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform

author: Editorial
description:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomati
title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
A tiny scar, bloodshot eyes and sagging jowls – it is the intimate details of these 15th-century masterpieces that make them so relatable today

The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026, but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves
title: The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human | Editorial

author: Maya Yang and Alfie Packham
description:
Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’

Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting.

While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida. GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more
title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI

author: Guardian sport
description:
Newcastle host Arsenal on Saturday while Mauricio Pochettino’s Manchester United visit Liverpool on Sunday

Saturday 12.30pm TNT Sports 1 Venue Etihad Stadium

Continue reading...
title: Premier League team news: predicted lineups for the weekend action

author: Jennifer Rankin and Peter Walker in Brussels
description:
Agreements reached on food and drink, emissions and to allow young people to move around continent, but may be derailed over student fees

Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides.

At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

Continue reading...
title: Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit

author: Jonathan Freedland
description:
From predatory male celebrities to ordinary men who connive to abuse women, there is no doubt where the problem lies – and the solution too

The only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a tax
title: After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides | Jonathan Freedland

author: Hannah Clugston
description:
Hepworth Wakefield, West Yorkshire
He spent over 60 years painting clowns, ringmasters and acrobats – and the results transport you to a dazzling magical world

At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable.

It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immed
title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review

author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
description:
Actor and author are alleged to have attacked and gang-raped a woman while filming together in 2018

French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot.

The alleged attack took place in December 2018 during the shooting of Thalasso, a film starring the two men as versions of themselves who meet at a health spa and have long philosophical conversations while in white bath-robes.

Continue reading...
title: Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq investigated over on-set rape and assault allegations

author: Caroline Davies
description:
Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s

Police are searching for a missing chemistry teacher convicted of sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s after she did not turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, was not found at her Hemel Hempstead home by Metropolitan police officers after her failure to attend Harrow crown court in north London on Friday, where a warrant was issued for her arrest.

Continue reading...
title: Police search for teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article about categories on the census form

It’s about time we fixed the Black English category in the census, whether popular or not (It’s absurd that ‘Black English’ is not on the census. We should be free to claim that identity if we choose, 14 November). Categories count. They make citizens, politically engineer belonging and allow people to be seen and to see themselves. The excuse that the Black English category is simply unpopular doesn’t wash. I remember in the 1990s when the Black British, or Black African categories were all the rage, they were never particularly comfortable to tick, but we all got over ourselves and stomached the flattening of our complex identities for what we believed was a good cause.

A Black English category would also help me out enormously, living as I do in France, where people don’t believe me when I
title: We should be free to call ourselves Black English | Letters

author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
description:
Mikka Anderson stockpiled weapons and tried to recruit accomplice for attack on Royal Hotel

A white supremacist has been found guilty of planning a firebomb terror attack on asylum seekers in Hull.

Mikka Anderson, 24, stockpiled weapons including napalm, knives and a crossbow for an assault designed to kill as many people as possible, Newcastle crown court heard.

Continue reading...
title: White supremacist convicted of planning bomb attack on asylum seekers in Hull

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Paul Keleher KC offers an insight into how juries are directed. Plus a letter from Prof Nicole Moreham

In your report (‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser, 15 November), Prof Katrin Hohl suggests that while significant progress has been made by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service, the court system was being left behind.

It seems to be little known that for many years judges have been trained to direct juries to ignore rape myths and direct them that many victims of sexual assault are unable to physically resist and often delay reporting the assault. Juries are directed that this should not cast doubt on their accounts of being assaulted.
title: Judges, juries and rape myths in trials | Letters

author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya, Turkey
description:
Fiona Harvey reads between the lines of the draft document that will end up outlining decisions and resolutions from the 31st climate summit

  • Cop31 live – latest updates

The final text is one of the most important documents that will come out of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. What emerges in the latest draft here is that it will not be a new treaty, but a series of decisions and resolutions. These decisions have legal force in the context of the Paris agreement, so this is a powerful document. But it is also a document that can be accepted only with the consensus of all parties, therefore much of the language is cautious and some is ambiguous or open to interpretation, to the frustration of countries who want to move faster.

I. Global progress and context
1. Strongly reaffirms commitment to multilatera
title: Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means

author: Ellie Violet Bramley
description:
From Jennifer Lawrence to Kate Moss, the fuzz-trimmed garments are proving popular with celebrities, while others are DIY-ing their way into the trend

While puffer jackets have dominated winter wardrobes for years, this winter an alternative is emerging: the fuzz-trimmed opera coat.

Originally worn over formal evening gowns, new interpretations come in both floor-grazing and cropped styles and are being worn with everything from minidresses to jeans.

Continue reading...
title: A textural moment: why the fashion world is falling in love with opera coats

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Estelle Herszenhorn says the food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, while Lily van den Broecke and Charlie Wartnaby share tea ideas

Rachel Dixon’s article (The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November) shows how we can make healthy food go further, and the opportunity is bigger than many of us realise. The food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, and much of it is good fruit and vegetables that could have been eaten.

It’s not just peel and stalks we bin. WRAP found that date labels on fres
title: It’s time we all made healthy food go further | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Responding to an article in the series The experts, Sally Billenness advocates wearing a mask and ensuring good ventilation. Plus, a letter by Caroline Clitter

“Stay hydrated”, “keep moisturised”, “go for a walk”, “be social”: while these are definitely good things for us to do, they are hardly the top of the list for avoiding winter ailments (Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments, 18 November). I am glad you have included vaccinations, but the two most useful things you can do don’t get a mention: wear a mask and ensure ventilation.

It’s flu season and airborne viruses such as Covid are still harming people, although as it is hardly ever reported you would not know it. People are being told
title: The best way to avoid winter illness | Letters

author: Guardian staff and agency
description:
Virginia judge says the US president’s pet project ​is ​a ‘rushed job’ ​that ‌lacks ​legal basis

A federal judge on Friday morning issued an injunction to block construction of ⁠Donald Trump’s ‌proposed so-called “triumphal arch” as a huge presence near some of the most famous and sacred sites of the Washington DC area.

The judge in Alexandria, Virginia ​said during a ⁠hearing ​on Friday that the US president’s pet project ​was ​a “rushed job” ​that ‌lacked ​a ​legal basis.

Continue reading...
title: Construction of ⁠Trump’s ‌proposed ‘triumphal arch’ blocked by judge

author: Lyndsey Winship
description:
Norwich Theatre Royal
Magic is sprinkled over Michael Pink’s elegant show, with the spirited score played by the Northern Ballet Sinfonia

It wouldn’t be the first time an ugly sister has stolen the show. Andrew Tomlinson is a hoot in Northern Ballet’s new Cinderella as a klutzy, vainglorious stepsister with a great line in lovably grotesque facial expressions. He certainly provides some panto-like festivity in the midst of an otherwise very nice ballet.

Getting its UK premiere, this pretty Cinderella is choreographed by Michael Pink, who was associate artistic director at Northern Ballet in the 1990s, and it feels very much like the Northern Ballet of old: accessible and enjoyable mainstream dance with clear storytelling. (It was originally made for Milwaukee Ballet, where Pink has been artistic director since 2002.)
title: You shall go to the panto! Northern Ballet’s Cinderella spices the fairytale with festive fun – and a sweet twist

author: Stuart Heritage
description:
The first lady’s two-part TV documentary is a dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment. Calling it thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry

Previously on Melania: earlier this year – either because it found her a compelling subject, or because it wanted to flatter the president before a potentially destructive upcoming antitrust trial – Amazon spent $75m (£57m) to make and market a theatrically released documentary about Melania Trump.

I’m telling you this for two reasons. First, because you didn’t watch the Melania film. Nobody did, except for journalists who sat in otherwise empty cinemas and (if reports are to believed) people who responded to Craigslist ads offering them $50 to see it. The second reason is because Melania is a
title: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space

author: David Smith in Washington
description:
The US president rated his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin as 12 out of 10 but China and Russia had the most to celebrate

He got by with a little help from his friends. Rebuked by millions of voters in a still resilient democracy, Donald Trump travelled to Asia this week and found comfort in the company of autocrats who still flatter him.

The US president, reduced to lame-duck status at home by a humiliating midterm election defeat, returned to the global stage in a meeting with two strongmen in Shenzhen, China, that critics described as a new low for America’s claim to moral authority.

Continue reading...
title: Friend zone: humiliated by US voters, Trump basks in company of autocrats

author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
description:
Activists in more than 20 countries demonstrate over cost of living, learning conditions and rising military spending

Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending.

Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.

Continue reading...
title: Young people across Europe stage coordinated ‘fight for our future’ protests

author: Ugo Monye
description:
New Zealand want to ease the pain of defeat by Wales but England’s squad depth will make them formidable opponents

I’ve heard it said that in New Zealand, 65% of people are rugby fans but 95% are All Blacks fans. Regardless of how accurate those numbers are, the sentiment is clear, and it explains why Dave Rennie said his players had “let the country down” by losing to Wales. A backlash is coming at Twickenham.

I spent some time with Kieran Read this week, one of the greatest All Blacks to play the game. He enjoyed some fine wins over England during his career but also suffered two defeats and clearly still carries those scars. The pain and anguish remain and, after
title: Expect a fearsome backlash from cornered All Blacks – but England must play with freedom | Ugo Monye

author: Gerard Meagher
description:
• Itoje calls for players and fans to respect referees

  • ‘There’s a line. There are things I wouldn’t do’

Maro Itoje has said he will never adopt a win-at-all-costs mentality as England captain as he prepares to lead his side against the All Blacks at Twickenham on Saturday after a week in sport dominated by Rassie Erasmus’s “match-fixing” rant and sandpapergate.

Itoje has called on his “very good” side to take the next step towards greatness by clinching back-to-back victories over the All Blacks for the first time since 2003 but, guided by his Christian faith and moral compass, he is adamant there are lines he will not cross.

Continue reading...
title: England reject win-at-all-costs mentality in chase for repeat win over All Blacks

author: Steven Morris
description:
Thomas sentenced to 15 months after admitting to criminal damage to vessel that had been carrying asylum seekers

The far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has been sentenced to 15 months in jail after slashing a dinghy that had been carrying asylum seekers in the Channel.

Thomas had taken a boat out to observe the occupants of a dinghy being assisted by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), Border Force and the French coastguard on 22 September.

Continue reading...
title: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing dinghy in Channel

author: Sarah Matthews
description:
We’ve rounded up the beauty and hair care offers that are actually worth it – all tried, tested and loved by us

• The best early Black Friday deals

Few of us may be able to justify the cost of a big-ticket TV this Black Friday, but beauty is one area where we can usually afford a treat or two. Thank you, lipstick effect. It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower.

But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups t
title: The best Black Friday beauty deals I’d actually buy, from LED face masks to skincare staples

author: Hayley Spencer
description:
From your bath to your bedroom, an experts’ guide to making your home a stylish sanctuary

We are in the midst of “staying-in season”, enduring cold days and long nights. But if your attempts at hibernation aren’t working, maybe the ambience is off. The gloomy winter months call for soft mood lighting, warmer textures and sunny colours to bring more joy into your home. From accessories that tell a story to the trending fabric trick to hide clutter, here are ways to create that elusive sense of cosiness this season. And I promise none of them involves buying yet another candle.

***

Continue reading...
title: Banish the big light: 12 interiors hacks for a cosy winter (and not a candle in sight)

author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
description:
The English seaside town tops the list for 16- to 24-year-olds out of work and education, but not for lack of young jobseekers’ efforts

Speaking random words like “cat” and “box” into her phone while filming herself in her pyjamas, Amy Butterworth’s relentless search for a job had reached a new level of absurdity.

The 19-year-old from Blackpool was applying for a role at Marks & Spencer, but first had to prove she was not a robot.

Continue reading...
title: ‘You can’t get experience if no one’s employing you’: the vicious circle facing Blackpool’s Neets

author: Matthew Weaver
description:
Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands

The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset.

Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory.

Continue reading...
title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death of woman at Somerset holiday park

author: Arifa Akbar
description:
Young Vic, London
Adaptation of Christian Kracht’s novel is full of heartwarming comedy as a mother and son take a trip to distribute ‘dirty money’ to good causes

You would be hard-pushed to find a more charismatic double act than Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw. She dazzles as a dowager, bringing flamboyant physical flourishes as she knocks back the cooking wine; he is her lugubrious son, Christian, a novelist with writer’s block. Their story trades on kookiness but the chemistry would keep you captivated even if they watched paint dry for the duration of this interval-free drama.

Based on Swiss author Christian Kracht’s bestselling novel, adapted by Colin Teevan, it is charmingly directed by Walter Meierjohann. The third big star is Lizzie Clachan’s set, so full of mischief that it is like a magician pulling out imaginative visual jokes and clever thrills and spills. Glyn Pritchard heroically plays ancillary roles (from taxi driver
title: Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter are a dynamite duo on the road to nowhere in Eurotrash

author: Talia Slonim
description:
People who arrive in Australia not having learned to swim often fear the water. For these Splash of Colour students, even blowing bubbles ‘is Everest’

In a public pool in Melbourne’s west, where the smell of chlorine hangs thick in the air, Dharmveer Kaur practises blowing bubbles in the shallow pool. Sounds echo across the enormous indoor aquatic centre, as people fresh from school and work mingle in the pools, spas and water slides. Kaur quietly concentrates on submerging her face in the water, following her instructor’s guidance in a lane away from the chaos.

To the young children taking swimming lessons in the lane beside her, the throngs of older men making their way to the spa, or the mother casually breastfeeding in the pool opposite her, Kaur’s bubble blowing may not seem remarkable. But for the woman who never learned to swim, it feels monumental.
title: ‘It gives me power’: the swimming class that’s changing lives

author: Kat Lay
description:
The US, Mexico and Bolivia this week joined the unenviable club of nations that have lost their measles-free status

Deaths caused by measles are not peaceful. In his hospital in Uganda, Dr Eric Wobudeya treats young infants after the virus has attacked their lungs and airways, or triggered pneumonia.

“These are children who are dying, and they are struggling for oxygen,” he said.

Continue reading...
title: ‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again

author: Andrew Pulver
description:
Was it all a dream? Has Bond been in hiding? Or will Robert Pattinson simply report to HR on his first day? Russell T Davies, David Hare and more give their takes

“James Bond will return,” says the closing title on No Time to Die, the most recent James Bond film and the final one to star Daniel Craig. It is just as well: Bond has to all appearances been vaporised by sea-launched missiles, having been infected by nanobots programmed to attack his nearest and dearest at the slightest touch. No one would believe that one of the world’s most successful film series would come to such an abrupt halt, but no doubt a little reassurance helped.

Nevertheless, the first order of business for scriptwriter Steven Knight and director Denis Villeneuve will be dealing with it: how to revive and re-energise a character at the heart of the action. Speculation on their best way forward has been rife, and previous examples are not hard to find. Sherlock Holmes was killed off by Arthur Cona
title: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?

author: Emma Brockes
description:
It’s a hard life for the Prince and Princess of Wales, but spare a thought too for jailed Bankman-Fried and the overlooked 007s

All eyes on China ahead of the trilateral summit this week, but it’s India and the three-day royal tour by the Prince and Princess of Wales that catches my eye. The couple arrive in Mumbai and as a steady stream of photos emanates from their back-to-back schedule, the usual question surfaces: how on earth do they stand it?

Continue reading...
title: Digested week: Pity the touring royals – and the hacks made to schlep around after them

author: Kevin Rawlinson
description:
Temperatures will be ‘severe’ in the north, as low as minus 9C, with some sub-zero temperatures farther south

Friday night will be the coldest night of the autumn so far, forecasters have said, surpassing the previous chilliest: Thursday.

A low of -8.4C was recorded at Tulloch Bridge in the Scottish Highlands overnight, according to the Met Office. Sub-zero temperatures were also recorded in Northern Ireland. More southerly areas stayed substantially warmer overnight on Thursday.

Continue reading...
title: Friday night will be ‘coldest of the autumn so far’, UK forecasters say

author: Jakub Krupa
description:
Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow

Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone are reported to have crashed in Poland during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it was “one of the largest attacks” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine.

Continue reading...
title: Russian missiles and drone reportedly hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine

author: Flora Willson
description:
Bridgewater Hall, Manchester
Thomas Adès, the Hallé and soloist Pekka Kuusisto gave the world premiere of Gabriella Smith’s violin concerto How to Be a Bird, plus a thrilling and fresh take on Stravinsky’s Firebird Suite

When did you last attend an orchestral concert in which the composers’ average age hovered around 30? Classical music loves prodigies, but these days they tend to be performers rather than composers. The high-stakes game of orchestral programming favours the experienced, not to mention the deceased. So how invigorating to encounter an entire concert that oozed youthful confidence, creative energy and moments of explosive swagger.

The opener was These Premises Are Alarmed, the miniature with maximalist ambitions composed for the Hallé’s inauguration of the Bridgewater Hall in 1996 by the then 25-year-old
title: Hallé/Adès/Kuusisto review – this concert oozed youthful confidence and creative energy

author: Press Association
description:
• Man accused of abusing former Bournemouth winger

  • Alleged incident happened at Anfield game in 2025

A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the Manchester City forward withdrew his support for the prosecution.

Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool magistrates court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the Premier League match between Liverpool and Semenyo’s former club Bournemouth at Anfield on 15 August last year.

Continue reading.
title: Liverpool fan found not guilty of racial abuse after Antoine Semenyo withdraws from case

author: Jonathan Jones
description:
Nan Goldin gets real, Eyck makes jaws drop, Ragnar Kjartansson revels in Sussex and Anselm Kiefer delivers a truckload of imaginative art – all in your weekly dispatch

Nan Goldin: You Never Did Anything Wrong
The great chronicler of real American lives fills the Hayward with passion and protest.
• Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November to 14 March

Continue reading...
title: Nan, Van, Ragnar and ‘the world’s greatest living artist’ – the week in art

author: Michael Hogan
description:
Dominic West and Sienna Miller’s divorce battle has made for a rollicking potboiler in prestige drama clothing. As it approaches its explosive finale, expect the show to become a TV fixture

A tech titan is brought down by the oldest trick in the book: a honeytrap. In the week that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, co-founder of the world’s most valuable chip company, worth a whopping $4tn (£3tn), resigned over revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, divorce drama War could hardly feel more timely.

That’s also how the HBO/Sky legal thriller begins. Billionaire social media mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West in textbook posh rotter mode) has a hotel tryst with an alluring stranger after an awards show. She turns out to be in cahoots with his wife, Hollywood star Carla Duval (played with icy glamour by Sienna Miller), to prove her husband’s infidelity. Missi
title: ‘If they play dirty, we’ll be total and utter filth’ Gasp-inducing sex-and-scandal drama War is here to stay

author: Eddy Frankel
description:
Malaysian cruisers overwhelm a gallery, a red balloonist is crushed by an orb, sneakers are brought back to life in someone’s basement and a woman makes a splash in a kids’ drink

★★★★☆

Continue reading...
title: From the Reeboks of a retired raver to a nude swim in a Monster Energy drink: four free exhibitions to see

author: Ali Martin at the Melbourne Cricket Ground
description:
Amid an increasingly febrile atmosphere in Australia, the white-ball captain is not expected at any press conferences

After a toe-curling, stonewalling press conference before the recent one-day series against England, Australia’s usually happy-go-lucky white-ball captain, Mitch Marsh, opted out of a repeat before the Twenty20s that start here on Saturday.

In his place came Victoria’s Sam Harper to talk about his looming debut at the MCG. A nice local angle, for sure, with the 29-year-old wicketkeeper having overcome some troubling concussions in the past. But also a touch optimistic if intended to switch the focus in Australia away from the sandpaper skip fire.

Continue reading...
title: Sandpaper and silence: Marsh hides away as England’s T20 winners roll into MCG

author: Fran Singh (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
description:
Federal judge says Brooke Rollins emails to 100,000 staff violates the first amendment but department says it may challenge ruling

  • Religious messages US agriculture secretary emailed to staff deemed unconstitutional

The incoming US senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said that he and Donald Trump are in agreement about ending foreign military aid to Israel – and he hopes to find more common ground with the US president when he takes office.

“I agree with the president – I can’t believe I’m saying that – that we need to end foreign military aid that is unconditional to Israel, as well as
title: Trump officials consider appeal after agriculture secretary’s religious emails ruled unconstitutional – US politics live

author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
description:
Lifelong guardianship ceremonies were announced in July as way to publicly affirm chosen connections

Allan was 14 years old and had been through eight foster families and a stint in a children’s home when he began living with foster carer Russ in Kettering – a move that would change the course of his life.

Russ, 63, fought for Allan to get the school placements he needed and took him to kickboxing every week, eventually joining in himself. When Allan turned 18, he moved out into his own flat, but the pair have stayed close.

Continue reading...
title: ‘You’ve got me for life’: first ceremonies in England cement care leavers’ relationships

author: Diane Taylor
description:
Woman, 24, says she cannot work and faces destitution after it was found her mother had no right to UK passport

A 24-year-old woman who was born and raised in London believing she was a UK citizen has been left in a state of shock after being told by authorities that she is not British.

After the Home Office recently discovered that the woman’s mother, who is from Jamaica, had no right to a British passport, she received a letter informing her her UK passport would be revoked on March 11, 2026. It was due to expire in 2031.

Continue reading...
title: Home Office tells woman born and raised in London she is not British

author: Zoe Watts
description:
Before Gisèle Pelicot and now Joanne Young, drug-facilitated rape was virtually unheard of. I now realise that my own horrific ordeal was not unique

Like many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way.

I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed with for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me.

Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounde
title: I, too, was raped by my partner while drugged and unconscious. There are more survivors than you think | Zoe Watts

author: Henrietta Moore
description:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme
title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

author: Bruce Schneier
description:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and
title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier

author: Stefanie Glinski
description:
Six months after the Bundibugyo strain swept through eastern DR Congo, Sylvain Kabona Tibasima is still trying to warn friends and family about the dangers of the virus

The day Birungi Nembe was born in a hospital in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, her mother, Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, 46, was diagnosed with Ebola. Sylvie died a week later, leaving behind her husband and nine children, including her newborn daughter.

But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. Few relatives attended; the risk of infection was just too high.

Continue reading...
title: Ebola killed 46 members of one man’s family. Now he is fighting to save the rest

author: Alice Vincent
description:
It’s hardly the most exciting aspect of gardening, but getting stuck in now will leave you reaping the benefits in the new year

I am going to do the thing that put me off every gardening book I read for the first few years of teaching myself how to garden, and smugly lecture about the importance of soil. But I thought it would be less painful in late November, that languid hinterland between the crisp crunch of bright autumn and the mania of Christmas. If you’d rather, I could bang on about tool-cleaning? Thought not.

I am currently evolving into my next method of composting and getting proper compost bays. When we moved in, we inherited a couple of tall plastic bins – or “Daleks” as my fellow columnist Claire Ratinon calls them. Considering I’ve paid very little attention to the compost for the past 15 months, aside from throwing all of our raw fruit and vegetable waste in there, along with leaves and some cardboard, they’ve cope
title: Garden composting may not be glamorous, but it brings rich rewards

author: Rachel Leingang
description:
Michigan senator-elect also secured a meeting with JD Vance, who called him a ‘terrible evil’ in lead-up to election

The incoming US senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said that he and Donald Trump are in agreement about ending foreign military aid to Israel – and he hopes to find more common ground with the US president when he takes office.

“I agree with the president – I can’t believe I’m saying that – that we need to end foreign military aid that is unconditional to Israel, as well as Egypt and Saudi Arabia and Pakistan,” the senator-elect said.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I agree with the president’: incoming senator Abdul El-Sayed seeks to help Trump end military aid to Israel

author: Andrew Pulver
description:
Argentinian co-directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco work hard to appear impartial in account that situates the game in a long continuum of conflict

Here is a football documentary that is a cut above the drain-clogging content that loiters in streaming platforms everywhere. Its subject is the World Cup quarter-final contest between Argentina and England in 1986, a game constantly replayed in the collective consciousness for the two never-to-be-forgotten moments contributed by Diego Maradona: the illicit “hand of God” goal that gave Argentina the lead, and then five minutes later his sublime second goal, for which he skipped past half a dozen of the England team before slotting the ball home with the outside of his foot. It was this second strike, voted in 2002 as Fifa’s goal of the century, that partly lanced the boil of English rage over Maradona’s outrageous che
title: The Match review – Lineker, Shilton et al look back at England’s ‘hand of God’ clash with Argentina

author: Guardian community team
description:
We’d like to hear people’s experiences of incidents of abuse while working in UK schools.

Since the pandemic, many schools have reported rising pupil violence, misogynistic abuse of female staff is on the increase, and teachers have observed a rise in problem parents.

We would like to hear from teachers about their experiences of seeing or being the victim of violence and abuse in schools, from either pupils or parents, within the last five years.

What happened and was the incident reported? If the police were involved, what was the outcome?

Please do not include any identifying details of the children involved.
title: UK teachers: have you experienced abuse in schools?

author: Ed Aarons
description:
• Zubimendi also out of Saturday’s game at Newcastle

  • Arteta imposes Fantasy Premier League ban after leak

Mikel Arteta has said Bukayo Saka may not return before Christmas as the Arsenal forward continues his rehabilitation from a thigh injury.

Saka has been out since limping off against Bayern Munich at the end of last month, and it is understood he has yet to resume light training. Arteta revealed more tests during the international break confirmed the England forward did not need surgery and that he was expected to be out for another four weeks.

Continue reading...
title: Bukayo Saka may not return for Arsenal before Christmas, Mikel Arteta admits

description:
Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down

  • Business live – latest updates

Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.

Continue reading...
title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off

author: David Smith
description:
With the release of a new David O Russell biopic about the coach turned commentator turned gaming icon, those who knew him best remember his singular career

Wearing his Oakland Raiders uniform and helmet, and gripping an orange traffic cone like a lance, Ted Hendricks rode into the training session on a roan horse and stopped at the 50-yard line. Some American football coaches might have reacted to the stunt with fury. But John Madden was unfazed.

“We needed some relief from the intense grind,” recalls Hendricks, 79, who had borrowed the horse from a nearby stable. “It was a spur of the moment idea, but put a smile on everyone’s face. All Coach said once I dismounted was, ‘All right guys, Ted’s here, let’s get started.’ But I know he got a kick out of it too – just from the look on his face and the comments he made later in interviews.”<
title: NFL legend John Madden’s unlikely, unfiltered brilliance: ‘Coach was indeed animated’

author: Garrison Lovely
description:
Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm

You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.

Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase. On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network
title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely

author: Compiled by Gail Fletcher
description:
After consulting on the production of the 1957 musical Funny Face, which was loosely based on his own life as a young photographer, Richard Avedon considered leaving photography behind to pursue film directing. Although he ultimately remained a photographer, his fascination with Hollywood and its ideals endured throughout his life.

Richard Avedon: Hollywood, a new exhibition, brings together more than 120 of Avedon’s iconic and rarely seen photographs of major Hollywood figures, including actors, directors, writers and composers, capturing the allure and influence of the entertainment industry.

The exhibition was curated by the Richard Avedon Foundation and is on view at Gagosian in Beverly Hills, California, through 19 December 2026

Continue reading...
title: Richard Avedon’s rarely seen portraits of Hollywood A-listers – in pictures

author: Hilary Osborne
description:
From cashback on what you buy to cut-price gift cards, we offer tips on how to maximise savings on your shopping

With Black Friday on the horizon, retailers are already offering discounts, and over the next few weeks you can expect to see more price cuts as they attempt to entice us to open our wallets.

It could be a great time to snap up the things on your Christmas list or buy household items you need yourself. And there are ways to maximise your savings on Black Friday – which this year falls on 27 November – by doubling up on discounts, or earning cashback on your purchases.

Continue reading...
title: Black Friday UK: how to make your bargain even better

author: As told to Anna Berrill
description:
‘Elbow noodles’ for a pet? Obsessed with labels, and jam-packed with condiments, it could only be author and chef Carla Lalli …

Cheese
I pretty much always have parm or grana padano, and pecorino, for pasta, Caesar salad or a dressing. I’ll have a parmesan rind in the mix, too, for when I’m cooking beans or grains. Then, there’s snacking cheese: sliced cheddar, Pepper Jack or muenster from the deli section for a quesadilla when Cosmo [Lalli’s son] gets home. I love mozzarella sticks for a protein snack, or sometimes when I’m alone, I’ll melt them on stir-fried rice with kimchi, or Korean rice cakes. I always have them in the summer when I go to the beach, too.

Marge’s food
This is my dog’s food. The usual recipe is a mix of ground minced turkey, minced beef, chicken liver, chicken gizzards, carrot, buttern
title: Chia pudding, pickle and picky dog food: whose fridge is this?

author: Andrew Lawrence
description:
The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric

Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out thre
title: Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent

author: Victoria Turk
description:
Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends

• The best eco-friendly baby products

Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need.

There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the
title: I’m a tech expert and new mum. Here’s what I learned testing 17 baby monitors

author: Guardian Staff
description:
The American novelist on the wild side of Maurice Sendak, re-evaluating Gone With the Wind, and the magical comforts of Alice Hoffman

My favourite book growing up
I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. Max’s visit to the land of monsters is escapist, of course, but there’s darkness and poetry in it, too. “The walls became the world all around” has always stuck with me.

The book that changed me as a teenager
A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living.

Continue reading...
title: Jodi Picoult: ‘Reading Ta-Nehisi Coates made me rethink racism’

author: Simon Jenkins
description:
In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September,
title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins

author: Dalya Alberge
description:
Exclusive: Guards told their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor that has rejected union recognition

The British Library has sparked outrage over plans to outsource its security workforce and hand over to a private company three of its public reading rooms, to be “repurposed” as business spaces for hire – despite having reportedly received millions of pounds from the public purse to refurbish those spaces.

Almost 70 guards have been told that their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor, STM, on 1 December. Their union, the PCS, has in turn been informed that STM has rejected union recognition for those staff.

Continue reading...
title: British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces

author: Simon Wardell
description:
A heart-shredding documentary about the beautiful friendship between Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell, and James McAvoy tells the cracking true story of two Scottish rappers pretending to be American

Emma Fogarty is 40 and lives with epidermolysis bullosa, a rare inherited disorder that makes her skin incredibly fragile, prone to tears and blisters. She’s also good mates with film star Colin Farrell. Rachel Fleit’s heart-shredding documentary follows their preparations for the 2024 Dublin marathon, which he plans to run before pushing her in a wheelchair for the final 4k. Fogarty’s resilience in the face of near-constant pain is inspirational but hard to watch, while Farrell reluctantly allows cameras into his private life, physically squirming at times as he opens up about his addictions, sons – one of whom also has a genetic condition – and his beauti
title: The Slightest Touch to California Schemin’: the seven best films to watch on TV this week

author: Safi Bugel
description:
(CDR)
Based around sounds recorded on her trips back to China, the Fujian-born, London-based producer creates a curious nocturnal collage on Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming

Lucid dreaming is one of the influences behind Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, the new record from Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z. “Every night is an adventure,” she writes in the liner notes, “I can even smell things in certain dreams.” The eight tracks here are suitably sensory, scattered with effervescent sounds, ephemeral whispers and polyrhythmic percussion.

Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which
title: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming

author: Alim Kheraj
description:
(EMI)
The pallid disco revivalism sounds like S Club 7 and the folksy stomp-clap like Mumford and Sons – yet a few standout moments prove they can still strike gold if they try

Listening to Wonderkids, the string-laden opener of Take That’s new album, it seems the three remaining fiftysomething boybanders are feeling reflective. “Forgiving you, forgiving me / This vicious circle is now complete,” sings Gary Barlow.

In the years since their last record, the band – and former member Robbie Williams – have indeed laid out the trials and tribulations of 35 years of Take That in several documentaries, some more candid than others. Earlier this year, they even embarked on a revival of their blockbuster 2009 Circus tour. Unfortunately, all this reminiscing has left their 10th album feeling so steeped in nostalgia that any moments of greatness struggle for attention.
title: Take That: Dreamers review – 50-something boyband fail to relight the fire on nostalgia-drenched return

author: Mark Sweney
description:
Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies

  • Business live – latest updates

Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to
title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring

author: Lyndsey Winship
description:
Sadler’s Wells, London
In Six Lethargies, Iván Pérez and Seirian Griffiths have devised a mammoth production of aching, ethereal sadness

‘If I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz. If they dance it, will we feel it?

Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer
title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat

author: Lauren Almeida
description:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

Yesterday Anthropic became one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world, ending its first day on the US stock market about 17% higher.

Chief executive Dario Amodei said the IPO “puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.”

The CSI 300 (-1.85%), Shanghai Composite (-2.10%), and Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 (-1.58%) are also posting notable declines. The downward momentum is continuing in futures with contracts on the S&P 500 (-0.50%), Nasdaq 100 (-0.98%) and Stoxx (-1.70%) all notably lower with Europe catching down.

The risk-off tone has also weighed on a wide variety of other asset classes, with gold (-2.68%) sliding to a 14-month low of $3,625/oz yesterday and down another -2.2% this morning. Bitcoin (-1.25%) has fallen to
title: Asian stocks headed for worst week since 2020 as Anthropic IPO fails to end AI rout – business live

author: Matthew Pearce
description:
Disagreements between rich polluting countries and everyone else threaten to push UN summit beyond its official end

Good morning. I’m Matthew Pearce, bringing you the Cop31 liveblog from London. Today is (supposedly) the final day of negotiations, and my colleagues on the ground will be guiding you through the conclusion of these contentious climate crisis talks.

Welcome to the final day of Cop31 in Antalya where the hosts Turkey and the president of negotiations, Australia, will bring the UN climate summit to a gentle and uneventful close and everyone will go home on time.

Continue reading...
title: Cop31 live: crunch time as deeply divided climate talks enter final day

author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
description:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase to £18bn.

Continue reading...
title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey

author: Hannah J Davies
description:
Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer lead a stunningly slick sci-fi miniseries, while The Celebrity Traitors’ smiling assassin tries out once-in-a-lifetime experiences with famous pals

Having finally bid farewell to teen saga Euphoria, Hunter Schafer has landed her first leading TV role. Her otherworldly looks and action chops are a perfect fit for this mega-budget miniseries loosely based on the work of Philip K Dick. She plays Cora, a human impersonating a member of the newly minted Replicant class. What follows is an exercise in stunning cyberpunk worldbuilding, executive produced by Ridley Scott and co-starring Michelle Yeoh as a Replicant in her final days. As talks are held in Brussels over closer relations, we examine the economic context and the challenges ahead

The UK and EU will hold the second summit since Brexit on Friday against a volatile economic backdrop.

Taking place in Brussels as the war in the Middle East hits the global economy, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will meet the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.

author: Felicity Halstead
description:
The focus seems to be on welfare reform as a way to deal with youth unemployment. But young people just want a fairer jobs market

  • Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low.

Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let the
title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead

author: Priya Elan
description:
The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today?

• Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood.

Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have em

description:
Bill takes in a chaotic quartet of student lodgers after his wife leaves him. Plus: the juicy divorce drama War concludes. Here’s what to watch this evening

9.30pm, BBC One

author: Guardian readers
description:
Last week we selected 50 players who are synonymous with their squad numbers. Our readers spotted notable absentees so came up with an alternative list, which does not start at No 1 or end at No 50

Which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers? We picked out 50 players last week who have come to embody the numbers on their backs. It was not an exhaustive list – as our readers have proved. We couldn’t include some legends of the game – Pelé and Lionel Messi for a start – and we missed a few brilliant stories. author: Michael White
description:
Cranbrook, Kent: Some species are absent, some have appeared twice – this may be a hangover from the summer drought and ‘second spring’

As autumn intensifies, it is easy for surface-dwellers such as ourselves to forget that we have already seen the trees turn once this year – not from shortening days, but for want of water. Summer turned leaves and meadows brown, until heavy rain in September and a second “spring” painted green all signs of the drought here in Kent, and banished at a stroke our fleeting interest in it.

Subterranean organisms, though, and those that span both worlds, have far longer memories. The boundary oak between the lower paddocks will now for ever have a narrow growth-ring within its girth, and fungi, to the human eye at least, have been sent into utter disarray.

Continue reading...
title: Country diary: It’s been a strange year for seasons – now our fungi are in disarray | Michael White

author: Chip St Clair
description:
After a childhood marked by horrifying cruelty, the day finally came when I held my father’s life in the balance

Growing up, I lived in fear of my father’s moods. If there was too much ice in his drink or the sofa cushions weren’t lined up, he’d fly into a rage. He’d call me names and smash my belongings. Once, he broke a dinner plate over Mom’s head. Still, she remained devoted to him.

My parents managed apartments in the US, so we moved around a lot. I never got to make friends, so I assumed all fathers were the same.

Continue reading...
title: Experience: I discovered my dad was a killer on the run – and turned him in

author: Zoe Williams
description:
Do teenagers need more protection from predatory adults? As campaigners in the UK call for changes to the law on consent, we talk to five people who became entangled with much older men and women

In the wake of the allegations against David Walliams (which he denies) – that he wooed young fans with promises of professional help – there have been renewed calls for a staggered age of consent. Sometimes called Romeo and Juliet laws, rules already exist in some US states, Canada and France to prevent “age-gap relationships” or, to put it another way, the sexual exploitation of teenagers by adults. The suggestion from UK campaigners Close the Consent Gap is for it to be illegal to have an age gap of more than three years if anyone is under 18, and last week, Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, called for
title: ‘I was drinking at 15, going to parties, being groomed and abused’: the grim reality of age-gap relationships

author: Graham Readfearn in Antalya
description:
As the UN summit nears its close, the ‘frustratingly’ slow progress and lack of focus on fossil fuel transition have the Pacific turning elsewhere for help

“I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.”

Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia.

Continue reading...
title: Pacific islanders face a ‘sickening disconnect’ between Cop31 and the climate devastation at their doorstep

author: Klaus Brinkbäumer
description:
As Andy Burnham pushes to reopen Brexit, Berlin won’t say it, but the truth is, we just want you back

Dear British friends,

Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja. Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing.

Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is an author and podcast and TV host in Germany

title: From Germany, with love: a letter to the UK | Klaus Brinkbäumer

author: Alexis Petridis
description:
From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas

Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”

It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 min
title: ‘We will become cyborgs!’ Peter Gabriel on bonobo ape duets, building a Jurassic Park for plants – and why AI will make great music

author: Arusa Qureshi
description:
In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play

At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash.

Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre.
title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum

author: Guardian sport
description:
Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys

After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United
title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
